title: Structural Adaptations
keyIdea: An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat. Structural adaptations are body parts and body shapes, such as a giraffe's long neck, an eagle's hooked beak and talons, or a dolphin's streamlined body. Behavioural adaptations are things an animal does, such as migrating or hibernating. Physiological adaptations are how the body works inside, such as antifreeze in the blood of Arctic cod. Each feature fits a job in a place: big thin ears lose heat in the desert, small ears keep it in the Arctic. Animals do not grow adaptations by trying or needing them. They build up over many generations, because animals born with helpful features survive and have more young.
familyTip: On a walk or at the zoo, play 'body, action or inside?'. Spot a feature, like a duck's flat bill or a squirrel burying nuts, say which kind of adaptation it is, then guess the job it does in that habitat.

visual.caption: What kind of adaptation is it? Drag each one to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort three kinds of adaptation, feed birds by beak shape, set fox ears for desert and Arctic, race shapes through water, build a snow animal.

kid: An adaptation is a feature that helps an animal survive where it lives. A body part or body shape is a structural adaptation. A giraffe's long neck reaches high leaves. An eagle's sharp talons grip its prey.

Some adaptations are things an animal does. Swallows fly south for the winter. Hedgehogs hibernate. These are behavioural. Others work inside the body, where you cannot see them. Arctic cod have antifreeze in their blood, so it does not freeze. These are physiological.

The shape of a body part fits its job. A finch's short, thick beak cracks seeds. A hummingbird's long, thin beak reaches into flowers. Big, thin ears let a desert fox lose heat. An Arctic fox has small ears to keep heat in. A dolphin's smooth, pointed shape slips through water.

Animals do not grow a feature because they need it or try hard. A giraffe that stretches its neck does not pass that on. Instead, young are born a little different from each other. The ones with helpful features live longer and have more young. Over many, many generations, the feature becomes common.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. The National Curriculum for England (Year 6, evolution and inheritance) asks pupils to show how animals and plants are adapted to their environment in different ways, and that adaptation may lead to evolution. NGSS 4-LS1-1 asks pupils to argue that internal and external structures support survival. The lab splits adaptations into structural, behavioural and physiological.

Every example was checked. Fennec fox ears (up to about 15 cm) help it lose heat and hear prey. Arctic foxes have short ears. Arctic cod make antifreeze proteins. Camels make small amounts of very concentrated urine to save water. Finch, hummingbird, eagle and duck beaks match seeds, nectar, meat and food strained from water. Streamlined bodies have less drag. The race in the lab shows the order of the shapes, not measured distances.

Common mistakes. Pupils think an animal adapts on purpose or within its lifetime, so the giraffe 'stretched its neck'. They call any feature 'structural', or mix up behaviour with body parts. They think big ears keep a fox warm. They think one animal can change its body to suit a new place. Each slip gets its own message in the lab.

practice.prompt: A giraffe's long neck is which kind of adaptation?
practice.hint: Is it a body part, something it does, or how the body works inside?
practice.explain: A neck is a body part, so it is structural. It lets giraffes reach leaves high in trees.

practice.prompt: Swallows fly thousands of kilometres south each autumn. Which kind of adaptation is this?
practice.hint: Is migrating a body part or something the bird does?
practice.explain: Migrating is something swallows do, so it is behavioural. It takes them to places with flying insects to eat.

practice.prompt: A desert fox's ear is {a} cm long. An Arctic fox's ear is {b} cm long. How many centimetres longer is the desert fox's ear?
practice.hint: Take the shorter length away from the longer one.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} cm. The longer ear gives off more body heat in the hot desert.

practice.prompt: Out of {n} young hares born in a snowy place, {w} are white and the rest are brown. How many are brown?
practice.hint: Take the white hares away from the total.
practice.explain: {n} − {w} = {=n-w} brown hares. Hunters spot brown hares on snow, so white hares are more likely to survive and have young. Over many generations, white fur becomes common.

practice.prompt: Which beak is best for sipping nectar from deep flowers?
practice.hint: The beak has to reach deep inside the flower.
practice.explain: A long, thin beak, like a hummingbird's, reaches deep into flowers. Short, thick beaks crack seeds; hooked beaks tear meat.

pool.prompt: Arctic cod have antifreeze in their blood. Which kind of adaptation is this?
pool.hint: You cannot see it. Is it about how the body works inside?
pool.explain: Antifreeze is a chemical made inside the body that stops the blood freezing, so it is physiological.

pool.prompt: Why does a desert fox have very big ears?
pool.hint: Ears are thin and full of blood vessels.
pool.explain: Blood flowing through big, thin ears loses heat to the air, which keeps the desert fox cool.

pool.prompt: Why do Arctic foxes have small ears?
choices: Big ears would freeze off at once
pool.hint: Think about what big ears do for the desert fox.
pool.explain: Small ears have less skin for heat to escape from, so the Arctic fox keeps its body heat.

pool.prompt: Which body shape lets an animal move through water most easily?
pool.hint: Think of a dolphin or a shark.
pool.explain: A streamlined shape lets water flow smoothly round it, so there is less drag. Dolphins, sharks and penguins all have it.

pool.prompt: How did giraffes come to have long necks?
choices: Over many generations, longer-necked giraffes survived and had more young
Each giraffe stretched its neck and passed that on
Giraffes decided they needed longer necks
pool.hint: Can a change made during one life be passed on?
pool.explain: Young giraffes are born slightly different. Those with longer necks reached more food, survived and passed the feature on. Over many generations it became common.

pool.prompt: A mountain hare lives in deep snow. Which set of features suits it?
choices: Thick white coat, small ears, wide furry feet
Thin brown coat, big ears, small bare feet
Thick brown coat, big ears, small bare feet
pool.hint: Think about staying warm, hiding on snow and walking on soft snow.
pool.explain: A thick coat keeps heat in, white hides it on snow, small ears lose less heat, and wide furry feet stop it sinking.

pool.prompt: A hedgehog hibernates through the winter. Which kind of adaptation is this?
pool.hint: Is hibernating a body part or something it does?
pool.explain: Hibernating is something the hedgehog does to survive winter when food is scarce, so it is behavioural.

pool.prompt: A swallow flies about {d} km a day on its migration south. How far does it fly in {n} days?
pool.hint: Multiply the distance for one day by the number of days.
pool.explain: {d} × {n} = {=d*n} km. Migrating is a behavioural adaptation: it takes swallows to places where flying insects are still plentiful.

pool.prompt: A group of {n} mountain hares has {w} white hares; the rest are brown. In the snow a fox catches {c} brown hares. How many brown hares are left?
pool.hint: First find how many are brown, then take away the ones caught.
pool.explain: {n} − {w} = {=n-w} brown hares, and {=n-w} − {c} = {=n-w-c} are left. White hares are harder to spot on snow, so more of them survive to have young.

pool.prompt: Which bird's beak is shaped for tearing meat?
pool.hint: Which beak has a sharp, curved tip?
pool.explain: A hooked, sharp beak tears meat. A finch's beak cracks seeds and a duck's bill strains food from water.
